title: imagemagick
description: ImageMagick is a free command-line suite for creating, converting, editing, and composing raster images across 200+ formats.

Getting Started.Getting Started:
This page covers installing ImageMagick and the one thing that trips
people up most: which command to actually type.

## 1. Install ImageMagick

| Platform | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Arch Linux | `sudo pacman -S imagemagick` |
| Debian / Ubuntu | `sudo apt install imagemagick` |
| Fedora | `sudo dnf install ImageMagick` |
| openSUSE | `sudo zypper install ImageMagick` |
| macOS (Homebrew) | `brew install imagemagick` |
| Windows | Install from the [official Windows binaries](https://imagemagick.org/script/download.php#windows) |

Verify it installed correctly:

```bash
magick -version
```

## 2. `magick` vs. `convert`

ImageMagick 7 consolidated its separate binaries (`convert`, `identify`,
`mogrify`, `composite`, `montage`, `compare`) into a single `magick`
command, used with a subcommand:

```bash
magick convert input.png output.jpg     # explicit subcommand form
magick input.png output.jpg             # convert is also the implicit default
magick identify photo.jpg               # print format/size/depth info
magick mogrify -resize 50% *.png        # in-place batch edit
```

On many Linux distributions the legacy standalone binaries (`convert`,
`mogrify`, etc.) are still installed for backward compatibility and behave
identically to `magick convert` / `magick mogrify`. If `convert` isn't found
on your system, or resolves to an unrelated program (this happens on some
Windows setups where `convert.exe` is a built-in disk utility), use the
`magick` form — it's also the form the project recommends going forward.
This guide uses `magick` throughout.

## 3. Run your first conversion

```bash
magick photo.heic photo.jpg      # convert by changing the output extension
magick photo.jpg -resize 50% small.jpg
```

ImageMagick infers input and output formats from file extensions by
default; you can override either with an explicit format prefix, e.g.
`magick png:-`  when piping through stdin/stdout.

## 4. Inspect an image before editing it

```bash
magick identify photo.jpg
# photo.jpg JPEG 4032x3024 4032x3024+0+0 8-bit sRGB 2.1MB 0.010u 0:00.009
magick identify -verbose photo.jpg | less
```

Continue to [Common Operations](/imagemagick/common-operations/) for
resizing, cropping, format conversion, and batch processing, or jump
straight to the [Command Reference](/imagemagick/command-reference/) for a
cheat sheet.

## The security policy file

Modern ImageMagick ships with a `policy.xml` that restricts certain
operations by default — most notably, reading/writing PDF and PS files
is often disabled out of the box on Linux distros, as a defense against a
class of past security issues. If a perfectly valid command fails with a
"not authorized" error, this is almost always why:

```bash
identify -list policy               # see current restrictions
sudo find / -name policy.xml 2>/dev/null   # locate the active policy file
```

See the [FAQ](/imagemagick/faq/) for how to safely loosen a
specific restriction rather than disabling the policy file entirely.

Core Concepts.Image Formats:
ImageMagick reads and writes well over 200 formats, but in practice
almost all real work involves a handful. Picking the right one for the job
matters more than any resize/quality flag.

## Raster vs. vector

ImageMagick is fundamentally a **raster** (pixel-grid) tool. It can
rasterize vector formats like SVG and PDF on read (converting curves/paths
into pixels at a chosen resolution), but it cannot edit vector paths as
vectors — for that you'd want Inkscape or a library like
`librsvg` directly.

```
# rasterize an SVG at a specific resolution — do this BEFORE resizing down,
# never render small then scale up
magick -density 300 in.svg out.png
```

`-density` must come *before* the input file, since it controls
how the vector source is rasterized, not how the resulting raster is
resized afterward.

## Lossy vs. lossless

| Format | Type | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| JPEG | Lossy | Photographs, no transparency needed |
| PNG | Lossless | Screenshots, graphics with transparency, sharp edges/text |
| WebP | Both (configurable) | Web delivery — smaller than JPEG/PNG at equal quality |
| AVIF | Both | Best-in-class compression; slower to encode, less universal support |
| TIFF | Usually lossless | Print, scanning, archival, layered/multi-page work |
| GIF | Lossless but 256-color palette | Short looping animations only |

Re-saving a lossy format repeatedly compounds quality loss (each
re-encode re-quantizes already-quantized data) — keep a lossless or
high-quality master and generate lossy derivatives from it, rather than
editing the lossy file directly across multiple sessions.

## Converting between formats

```bash
magick in.png out.jpg              # format is inferred from the extension
magick in.jpg out.webp
magick in.jpg -quality 90 out.avif
```

ImageMagick infers format from the file extension by default; to be
explicit (useful in scripts, or when writing to stdout) prefix with a
format name and colon:

```bash
magick in.jpg jpg:- > /dev/stdout
```

## Animated formats

```bash
magick frame*.png -delay 10 -loop 0 out.gif    # 10 = 1/10s per frame, loop 0 = infinite
magick out.gif -coalesce out_frames_%02d.png    # explode an animation back into frames
```

Animated WebP is generally preferred over GIF today — smaller files
at full 24-bit color instead of GIF's 256-color palette limit — but GIF
remains the most universally supported animated format across chat apps
and older tooling.

## Inspecting a file's actual format

```bash
identify -verbose in.jpg | head -30
identify -format "%m %wx%h %[colorspace]\n" in.jpg
```

Don't trust a file extension — a mislabeled file is common enough
that `identify` (which inspects the actual header bytes) is worth
running before batch-processing files from an untrusted or unknown
source.
Core Concepts.Color & Channels:
Most color problems in ImageMagick — washed-out output, unexpected
transparency, wrong colors after conversion — trace back to color
space or channel handling, not the operation you were actually trying to
do.

## Color spaces

```bash
magick in.jpg -colorspace Gray out.jpg        # grayscale
magick in.jpg -colorspace CMYK out.tiff       # for print workflows
identify -format "%[colorspace]\n" in.jpg     # check current colorspace
```

A common trap: converting to grayscale by simply averaging RGB channels
(what naive tools do) looks noticeably different from a proper perceptual
grayscale conversion. ImageMagick's `-colorspace Gray` uses
perceptual luminance weighting by default, which is almost always what you
actually want.

## Extracting and manipulating channels

```bash
magick in.png -channel R -separate red_channel.png    # extract just the red channel
magick in.png -alpha extract alpha_mask.png            # extract the alpha channel as a grayscale mask
magick in.png -channel RGB -negate out.png              # invert color, leave alpha untouched
```

## Transparency & alpha

```bash
magick in.png -transparent white out.png      # make white pixels fully transparent
magick in.png -fuzz 10% -transparent white out.png   # also catch near-white (anti-aliased edges)
magick in.png -background none -flatten out.png       # flatten layers onto a transparent background
```

`-fuzz` sets a color-distance tolerance for operations like
`-transparent` that would otherwise only match an exact color
— essential for real-world images where anti-aliasing means "white"
pixels are rarely pure `#FFFFFF`.

## ICC color profiles

```bash
identify -verbose in.jpg | grep -i profile           # check for an embedded profile
magick in.jpg -profile sRGB.icc out.jpg               # assign/convert to a specific profile
magick in.jpg -strip out.jpg                          # remove the profile entirely (smaller file)
```

Photos from cameras and design tools often carry a wide-gamut profile
(Adobe RGB, ProPhoto RGB). Browsers mostly assume sRGB, so converting
(not just stripping) to sRGB before web delivery avoids colors looking
duller or shifted than intended:

```bash
magick in.jpg -profile AdobeRGB.icc -profile sRGB.icc out.jpg
```

## Quick reference

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-colorspace <space>` | Convert color space (Gray, CMYK, sRGB, HSL, …) |
| `-channel <R|G|B|A|RGB|...>` | Restrict following operations to specific channels |
| `-separate` | Split channels into individual grayscale images |
| `-fuzz N%` | Color-distance tolerance for color-matching operations |
| `-transparent <color>` | Make a matching color fully transparent |
| `-profile <file.icc>` | Assign or convert to an ICC color profile |

Common Tasks.Common Operations:
The everyday operations you'll reach for most: resizing, cropping,
converting formats, and running the same edit across many files at once.

## Resizing

```bash
magick in.jpg -resize 50% out.jpg          # scale by percentage
magick in.jpg -resize 800x600 out.jpg      # fit within a box, keep aspect ratio
magick in.jpg -resize 800x600! out.jpg     # force exact size, ignore aspect ratio
magick in.jpg -resize 800x out.jpg         # fixed width, height auto
magick in.jpg -resize 'x600' out.jpg       # fixed height, width auto
magick in.jpg -resize 800x600^ out.jpg     # fill the box, may overflow one dimension
```

By default `-resize` only ever scales *down*; add `>` after the geometry
(e.g. `800x600>`) to make that explicit, or `<` to only scale up.

## Cropping

```bash
magick in.jpg -crop 400x400+100+50 out.jpg   # width x height + x-offset + y-offset
magick in.jpg -gravity center -crop 500x500+0+0 out.jpg  # crop centered
```

The offsets are measured from the top-left corner unless `-gravity`
changes the anchor point.

## Rotating & flipping

```bash
magick in.jpg -rotate 90 out.jpg     # rotate clockwise
magick in.jpg -rotate -90 out.jpg    # rotate counter-clockwise
magick in.jpg -flip out.jpg          # vertical flip
magick in.jpg -flop out.jpg          # horizontal flip
magick in.jpg -auto-orient out.jpg   # apply EXIF orientation, then strip it
```

## Converting between formats

```bash
magick photo.png photo.jpg            # format is inferred from the extension
magick photo.jpg -quality 85 photo.jpg  # re-encode a JPEG at 85% quality
magick icon.png icon.ico              # works for icon/multi-frame formats too
magick animation.gif frame_%02d.png   # explode an animated GIF into numbered frames
magick frame_*.png animation.gif      # and the reverse: frames into a GIF
```

## Compressing & re-encoding

```bash
magick in.jpg -quality 75 out.jpg          # lossy JPEG/WebP quality (0-100)
magick in.png -strip out.png               # drop EXIF/ICC metadata to shrink the file
magick in.jpg -define jpeg:extent=200KB out.jpg  # target a max file size
```

## Watermarking & compositing

```bash
magick composite -gravity southeast -geometry +20+20 \
  watermark.png photo.jpg out.jpg
magick photo.jpg watermark.png -gravity center -composite out.jpg
```

Both forms overlay one image on another; `-gravity` picks the anchor
corner and `-geometry +x+y` nudges it in from that anchor.

## Adding text

```bash
magick photo.jpg -gravity south -pointsize 36 -fill white \
  -annotate +0+20 "Caption text" out.jpg
```

## Batch processing with `mogrify`

`mogrify` applies an operation to many files **in place** (it overwrites
the originals unless you pass `-path` to send output elsewhere) — useful
for bulk resizing or re-encoding a whole folder:

```bash
magick mogrify -resize 1600x1600\> *.jpg          # shrink oversized images only
magick mogrify -format webp -path out/ *.png       # convert a folder to WebP, keep originals
magick mogrify -strip -quality 80 *.jpg            # strip metadata + recompress, in place
```

Always test destructive `mogrify` runs on a copy first, or use `-path` to
write to a separate output directory.

## Contact sheets with `montage`

```bash
magick montage *.jpg -tile 4x -geometry 200x200+5+5 contact-sheet.jpg
```

Arranges a set of images into a grid — handy for thumbnails or a quick
visual index of a folder.

## Stripping metadata & optimizing for the web

```
# remove EXIF/ICC/comments — smaller file, also strips potentially sensitive metadata like GPS location
magick in.jpg -strip out.jpg

# a solid default recipe for web images
magick in.jpg -strip -interlace Plane -quality 85 -sampling-factor 4:2:0 out.jpg
```

`-interlace Plane` produces a progressive JPEG (renders a blurry
full preview immediately, sharpening as more data loads) instead of the
default top-to-bottom baseline scan — generally preferred for web
delivery.

## -thumbnail vs -resize

```bash
magick in.jpg -thumbnail 200x200 out.jpg
```

`-thumbnail` is a faster, lower-quality resize that also strips
profiles automatically — purpose-built for generating many small
preview images quickly. `-resize` applies the configured filter more
carefully and keeps metadata, which matters more for a final, full-size
output.
Common Tasks.Compositing & Layers:
Compositing combines two or more images using a mathematical rule (an
"operator") that decides how each pair of overlapping pixels blends. This
is how watermarking, masking, and Photoshop-style blend modes are done
from the command line.

## Basic compositing

```
# place logo.png on top of base.png at (10,10)
magick base.png logo.png -geometry +10+10 -composite out.png

# centered
magick base.png logo.png -gravity center -composite out.png
```

The default operator is **Over** — the top image's opaque
pixels replace the bottom's, and semi-transparent pixels blend
proportionally. This is what "watermark" or "sticker onto photo" almost
always means.

## Compositing operators (blend modes)

| Operator | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Over (default) | Standard alpha-blended overlay |
| Multiply | Darkens; white has no effect, black stays black — good for shadows/textures |
| Screen | Lightens; opposite of Multiply — good for light/glow effects |
| DstOut | Cuts a hole in the bottom image wherever the top image is opaque |
| CopyOpacity | Uses the top image's grayscale values as an alpha mask for the bottom |

```bash
magick base.png overlay.png -compose Multiply -composite out.png
```

## Masking with CopyOpacity

```
# mask.png: white = visible, black = hidden, grays = partial
magick photo.png mask.png -alpha off -compose CopyOpacity -composite out.png
```

This is the standard technique for non-rectangular crops (vignettes,
rounded shapes, gradient fades) — draw or generate a grayscale mask
image, then apply it as the alpha channel of the target rather than trying
to erase pixels directly.

## Tiling a watermark across an image

```bash
magick base.png \( logo.png -alpha set -channel A -evaluate multiply 0.3 +channel \) \
  -compose over -tile out.png
```

The parenthesized group `\( ... \)` is ImageMagick's way of
processing an image in an isolated sub-pipeline before it's used by the
outer command — here, reducing the logo's opacity to 30% before
tiling it repeatedly across the base image.

## Flattening multi-layer files (PSD, layered TIFF)

```bash
magick in.psd -flatten out.png              # merge all layers into one flat image
magick in.psd[0] out.png                    # extract just the first layer, unflattened
identify in.psd                             # list how many layers/frames a file contains
```

## Quick reference

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-composite` | Composite the last two images read |
| `-compose <op>` | Set the compositing operator (Over, Multiply, Screen, …) |
| `-gravity <dir>` | Anchor point for the composite |
| `-geometry +X+Y` | Explicit offset for the composite |
| `-tile` | Repeat the top image across the whole canvas |
| `-flatten` | Merge all layers/frames into a single flat image |
Common Tasks.Text & Drawing:
ImageMagick can annotate images with text and draw vector primitives
directly from the command line, or via MVG (Magick Vector Graphics) for
anything more precise than a single `-draw` flag can comfortably
express.

## Adding text

```bash
magick in.png -gravity south -pointsize 36 -fill white \
  -annotate +0+20 "Photo credit: psdk" out.png
```

`-gravity` sets the anchor point for the `+X+Y` offset that
follows — `south` anchors to the bottom-center, so
`+0+20` means "centered horizontally, 20px up from the bottom edge."

## Legible text over busy backgrounds

```bash
magick in.png -gravity south -pointsize 36 \
  -fill white -stroke black -strokewidth 2 \
  -annotate +0+20 "Readable on any background" out.png
```

A stroke outline (or a semi-transparent box behind the text — draw a
rectangle with `-fill 'rgba(0,0,0,0.5)'` first) keeps captions
legible regardless of what's underneath, which plain white/black fill
alone can't guarantee.

## Choosing a font

```bash
magick -list font                          # fonts ImageMagick knows about by name
magick in.png -font "DejaVu-Sans-Bold" -pointsize 40 \
  -annotate +10+50 "Custom font" out.png
# or point directly at a font file
magick in.png -font /usr/share/fonts/TTF/Inter-Bold.ttf \
  -pointsize 40 -annotate +10+50 "Custom font" out.png
```

## Drawing shapes

```bash
magick in.png -fill none -stroke red -strokewidth 3 \
  -draw "rectangle 50,50 200,150" out.png

magick in.png -fill "rgba(255,0,0,0.4)" \
  -draw "circle 100,100 100,150" out.png
```

`-fill none` draws an outline only; a fill color (including
alpha, as with `rgba()`) draws a filled shape instead.

## MVG for complex vector drawing

For anything beyond a shape or two, MVG (a small SVG-like language) read
from a file is far more maintainable than one long `-draw` string:

```
# scene.mvg
push graphic-context
  fill blue
  rectangle 20,20 180,80
  fill white
  font-size 24
  text 30,60 'Hello'
pop graphic-context
```

```bash
magick -size 200x100 xc:white -draw "@scene.mvg" out.png
```

`push`/`pop graphic-context` saves and restores drawing state
(fill, stroke, font) the same way SVG or a Canvas 2D context would, letting
you nest styled groups without each primitive needing to repeat every
style attribute.

## Quick reference

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-annotate +X+Y "text"` | Draw text at an offset from the gravity anchor |
| `-pointsize N` | Font size |
| `-font <name|path>` | Choose a font |
| `-fill` / `-stroke` | Fill / outline color for text and shapes |
| `-draw "<primitive>"` | Draw a rectangle, circle, line, polygon, path, etc. |
| `-draw "@file.mvg"` | Run a whole MVG drawing script |

Advanced.Scripting & Batch Processing:
Working on one image at a time doesn't scale. ImageMagick has a
purpose-built in-place batch tool (`mogrify`), plus works fine from
ordinary shell loops and scripts for anything more custom.

## mogrify: in-place batch operations

```
# resize every jpg in the current directory, overwriting each in place
mogrify -resize 50% *.jpg

# safer: write results to a separate directory instead of overwriting
mkdir resized && mogrify -path resized -resize 50% *.jpg

# convert an entire directory of PNGs to JPEG
mogrify -path jpg-out -format jpg *.png
```

`mogrify` is the odd one out among ImageMagick's commands: unlike
`magick`, which always reads an input and writes a distinct output,
`mogrify` modifies files where they are unless `-path` is given
— make sure that's actually what you want before running it on
originals you don't have backed up.

## Shell loops for custom per-file logic

```
for f in *.jpg; do
  magick "$f" -resize 1200x1200\> -quality 85 "optimized/$f"
done
```

`1200x1200>` (the trailing `>`) means "resize only if larger
than this — never upscale," a common requirement when normalizing a mixed
batch of user-uploaded images of unknown size.

## Parallelizing across cores

```bash
ls *.jpg | xargs -P4 -I{} magick {} -resize 50% "resized-{}"
# or, with GNU parallel:
ls *.jpg | parallel -j4 magick {} -resize 50% resized-{}
```

ImageMagick processes one file per invocation single-threaded (aside
from some internally multi-threaded operations), so for large batches,
running several `magick`/`mogrify` processes concurrently —
bounded to your core count — is the most effective speedup.

## Calling ImageMagick from Dart

```dart
import 'dart:io';

Future<void> resizeAll(List<String> files, String outDir) async {
  await Directory(outDir).create(recursive: true);
  final futures = files.map((f) {
    final out = '$outDir/${f.split('/').last}';
    return Process.run('magick', [f, '-resize', '50%', out]);
  });
  final results = await Future.wait(futures);
  for (final r in results) {
    if (r.exitCode != 0) {
      stderr.writeln('Failed: ${r.stderr}');
    }
  }
}
```

`Future.wait` over several `Process.run` calls gives you the
same "several processes at once" parallelism as the shell examples above,
without needing an external tool like GNU parallel.

## Multi-step pipelines with a manifest

For repeatable, documented pipelines (rather than a one-off shell loop),
a small script that reads a manifest is easier to maintain and re-run:

```
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
while IFS=, read -r src size quality; do
  magick "$src" -resize "$size" -quality "$quality" "out/$(basename "$src")"
done < manifest.csv
```

`set -euo pipefail` is worth having in any batch script: it stops
the whole run on the first failure instead of silently skipping a broken
file and continuing, which is usually the wrong default for anything you
plan to trust unattended.
Advanced.Montage & Collage:
`montage` arranges multiple images into a single grid — contact
sheets, thumbnail grids, before/after comparisons — in one command,
without you having to compute positions by hand.

## A basic contact sheet

```bash
magick montage *.jpg -tile 4x -geometry 200x200+5+5 contact-sheet.jpg
```

`-tile 4x` means 4 columns, as many rows as needed;
`-geometry 200x200+5+5` sets each cell to fit within 200×200 with
5px horizontal and vertical spacing between cells.

## Labeling each tile

```bash
magick montage *.jpg -tile 4x -geometry 200x200+5+5 \
  -label '%f' -pointsize 14 contact-sheet.jpg
```

`%f` in `-label` is a percent escape that expands to each
source file's name automatically — see
[Scripting & Batch
Processing](/imagemagick/scripting-batch-processing/) for more on driving this from a script over a large,
changing set of files.

## A fixed grid with consistent tile size

```
# force every image to fill its cell exactly, cropping as needed
magick montage *.jpg -tile 3x3 -geometry 150x150^+2+2 \
  -gravity center -extent 150x150 grid.jpg
```

Plain `-geometry` fits images within a cell, which can leave
uneven whitespace for images of different aspect ratios. The
`^` modifier plus `-extent` instead fills and crops each tile
to an identical size, useful when the source images vary in dimensions but
the grid needs to look uniform.

## Side-by-side before/after comparisons

```bash
magick montage before.jpg after.jpg -tile 2x1 -geometry +10+0 \
  -label '%f' compare.jpg
```

## Building a GIF from a directory of frames

```bash
magick -delay 20 -loop 0 frame*.png animation.gif
```

This isn't a montage (frames aren't arranged spatially) but it's the
same underlying idea — combining many separate images into one output
— and is covered in more depth, including format tradeoffs, in
[Image Formats](/imagemagick/image-formats/).

## Quick reference

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-tile CxR` | Grid layout: C columns, R rows (either can be left blank/auto) |
| `-geometry WxH+X+Y` | Per-tile size and spacing |
| `-geometry WxH^+X+Y -extent WxH` | Fill and crop each tile to an identical size |
| `-label '%f'` | Caption each tile with its source filename |
| `-background <color>` | Set the color behind/between tiles |

| `-gravity center` | Anchor point for composite/annotate/extent operations |
| `-annotate +X+Y "text"` | Draw text at an offset |
| `-draw "circle X,Y X2,Y2"` | Draw a primitive shape |
| `magick montage *.jpg -tile 4x -geometry 200x200+5+5 out.jpg` | Build a contact sheet |
| `mogrify -path out/ -resize 50% *.jpg` | Batch-resize into a separate output directory |
Reference.FAQ:
## Should I use `magick` or `convert`?

Use `magick` (as in `magick convert ...` or the shorthand
`magick in.jpg out.png`) on any current install — it's the unified entry
point introduced in ImageMagick 7 and is what the project recommends. The
standalone `convert` binary still exists on many distros for backward
compatibility and behaves the same way, but it may eventually be removed,
and on some systems (notably some Windows setups) `convert` resolves to an
unrelated built-in tool.

## What's the difference between `-resize` and `-thumbnail`?

They both scale an image, but `-thumbnail` is a faster, lower-quality
shortcut intended for generating small previews: it skips some filtering
steps and automatically strips embedded color profiles and metadata.
Use `-resize` when output quality matters (e.g. a resized photo for
publishing) and `-thumbnail` when generating many small preview images
quickly.

## Can I resize a JPEG without any quality loss?

Not with a true resize — resizing always resamples pixels, and
re-encoding a JPEG is inherently lossy. What you *can* do losslessly is
crop and rotate by multiples of 90°, using `-crop` together with
`+repage`, since those operations can work on whole JPEG blocks without
re-encoding pixel data. For genuinely lossless resizing, convert to a
lossless format (PNG, WebP lossless) first.

## Why do I get a "not authorized" / policy error converting a PDF?

Many distributions ship a `policy.xml` (usually at
`/etc/ImageMagick-7/policy.xml`) that disables certain coders — PDF and
PS/EPS in particular — by default, as a security hardening measure
against maliciously crafted files (this followed a real vulnerability
class dubbed "ImageTragick" in 2016). If you trust your inputs, find the
relevant `<policy domain="coder" rights="none" pattern="PDF" />` line and
change `rights="none"` to `rights="read|write"`.

## Why did my GIF lose its animation after editing?

Most single-image operations (like a plain `-resize`) only touch the
first frame by default. Add `-coalesce` before the operation to expand
every frame to full size first, and `-layers optimize` after it to
re-compress the result back into an efficient animated GIF:

```bash
magick in.gif -coalesce -resize 50% -layers optimize out.gif
```

## ImageMagick is using huge amounts of memory/disk on a large image. Why?

ImageMagick decodes images to an uncompressed pixel cache, which can be
far larger than the source file, and it will spill that cache to disk
(`/tmp` by default) once memory limits are hit. For very large images or
batch jobs, raise or lower the relevant limits explicitly with
`-limit memory 2GiB` / `-limit disk 4GiB`, or process files one at a time
instead of globbing an entire folder into one command.

## A few more common questions

**I got a "not authorized" error on a PDF/PS file — how do I fix it?**  
That's `policy.xml` blocking the coder, usually as a security
default on Linux distros. Find the active policy file
(`identify -list policy` shows the path context) and change the
relevant `<policy domain="coder" rights="none" pattern="PDF" />`
line's `rights` to `read` or `read|write` rather than
deleting the whole file, which would remove other, unrelated protections
too.

**Why did resizing make my PNG blurry?**  
The default resize filter is tuned for photographic content. For sharp
UI/pixel-art graphics, disable filtering and blending explicitly:
`magick in.png -filter point -resize 200% out.png`.

**convert vs magick vs mogrify — what's the real difference?**  
`magick` is the modern unified entry point (v7+) and should be
preferred; `convert` is the legacy v6 name for the same
read-transform-write operation kept for compatibility. `mogrify` is
different in kind: it modifies files *in place* (or into
`-path`) rather than producing a new output path, which is what
makes it suited to batch operations — see
[Scripting & Batch
Processing](/imagemagick/scripting-batch-processing/).
